title: handoff
summary_easy: handoff is a supervisor for incident response agents where every request for human approval has an owner, a deadline, and a rule written in advance for what happens if nobody answers. On silence it can drop the action, run a safer substitute, ask the next tier, or freeze, and it never treats silence as approval. It has 212 tests, 11 scenarios, and no dependencies, and it runs on a simulated cluster with rule based workers.
summary_deep: A hand written supervisor state machine (plan, dispatch, aggregate, decide, act, verify) fans an incident out to five deterministic workers holding a read only tool registry, so only the supervisor can execute. The aggregator tracks supporters and detractors per hypothesis; a hypothesis with voices on both sides is contested, and any action addressing it has its effective risk raised one level. A risk keyed policy table (medium 300 s escalate, high 180 s safe_fallback, critical 600 s hold with quorum 2) drives an escalation engine that routes by tier, skill, and load, halves later windows with a 30 second floor, and fires deadlines on a caller driven tick against an injected clock. OnExpiry has four members and deliberately no ALLOW; safe_fallback runs a tool's declared, import validated, strictly lower risk substitute, such as read only mode for a database failover. Config mistakes are refused at load, decisions cover approve, reject, modify, and defer, and every state change goes to an append only journal. 212 unittest cases and 11 YAML scenarios run on a bare interpreter in under a tenth of a second across Python 3.11 to 3.13; the suite caught a safety branch that was unreachable and a risk bump discarded at rule lookup. Open gaps: no scheduler, no persistence, no resume from a frozen run, and no LLM workers.

sheet.easy:
## handoff in one line
Agents that need a human's approval, where every request has an owner, a deadline, and a written rule for what happens if nobody answers.

## Why it matters
Most approval prompts wait forever. At 3am nobody answers, and an incident with a parked agent has nobody watching it.

## How it works
- A **supervisor** sends five read only workers to investigate, merges what they say, and proposes fixes, cheapest first.
- Cheap actions run on their own. Medium and above go to an **escalation engine**.
- The engine pages the right person (tier, skill, load) with a **deadline**.
- On silence it does one of four things: **deny**, **safe fallback**, **escalate** to the next tier, or **hold**. There is no **allow**.
- If workers **disagree**, the fix is treated as one level riskier, so it asks a human.
- Every step goes into an append only **journal**.

## The policy
| Risk | Ask? | First deadline | On silence | Sign offs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| read only, low | no | none | deny | 1 |
| medium | yes | 300 s | escalate | 1 |
| high | yes | 180 s | safe fallback | 1 |
| critical | yes | 600 s | hold | 2 |

## The story to tell
Failover proposed, Ana paged with 180 seconds, nobody answers, the database goes read only instead. Nothing lost, reversible, and the log says nobody answered.

## Numbers
212 tests, 11 scenarios, 0 dependencies, under a tenth of a second, CI on Python 3.11 to 3.13. Simulated cluster, rule based workers.

## Honest gaps
No scheduler for the deadline tick, no pager attached, static seven person roster, no LLM workers, frozen incidents cannot resume.
sheet.deep:
## Architecture
```
Incident -> Supervisor (only executor)
  PLANNING     static plan: logs, metrics, replication, runbook -> remediation (depends on all 4)
  DISPATCHING  workers get a READ_ONLY-filtered ToolRegistry
  AGGREGATING  support/against per hypothesis, supporters/detractors, CONFLICT_DETECTED
  DECIDING     drop proposals not addressing confirmed or contested hypotheses
  ACTING       effective risk -> forbids? -> needs_human? -> raise_for -> AWAITING_HUMAN | execute
  VERIFYING    read_metrics: p99 <= 1000 ms resolves; else next action or ABANDONED
Terminal: RESOLVED, FROZEN, ABANDONED. advance() loop guard: 100.
EscalationEngine: raise_for, decide, tick, open; Roster; Policy; Journal (append only, JSONL sink, subscribers)
```
Layers: core (no deps) <- bus, tools <- agents, escalation <- supervisor <- evalsvc. Everything constructor injected by system.build().

## Escalation record
incident_id, tool, args, risk (effective), reason, blast_radius, ladder, deadline_seconds, on_expiry, quorum, required_skill, safe_fallback, state, tier_index, attempts[tier, responder_id, assigned_at, deadline, answered, decision, note], approvals, modified_args, resolved_at, resolution_note. Owner = latest attempt's responder.

## Policy (config/policy.yaml), autonomy guarded, escalate_at_or_above medium
| risk | approval | deadline | on_expiry | quorum | ladder | skill |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| read_only | no | 0 | deny | 1 | none | none |
| low | no | 0 | deny | 1 | none | none |
| medium | yes | 300 | escalate | 1 | primary, secondary | none |
| high | yes | 180 | safe_fallback | 1 | primary, secondary, incident_commander | infrastructure |
| critical | yes | 600 | hold | 2 | incident_commander, engineering_manager, director | infrastructure |

Tier window: $w_k = \max(30, \lfloor d \cdot 0.5^{k} \rfloor)$ s. Medium 300, 150. High 180, 90, 45. Critical 600, 300, 150 (arithmetic from the code).

## OnExpiry, exactly
| value | state | effect |
|---|---|---|
| deny | DENIED_ON_TIMEOUT | action dropped, ACTION_DENIED, run continues |
| safe_fallback | FELL_BACK (or DENIED_ON_TIMEOUT if none declared) | fallback runs with args narrowed to its fields, approved_by "timeout fallback" |
| escalate | ASSIGNED on next tier, or EXHAUSTED | unanswered attempt kept, shorter window |
| hold | HELD (open, never fires again) | INCIDENT_FROZEN, run goes FROZEN |
No ALLOW: rejected at load, asserted absent by test. The original high risk action only ever runs with a human approval.

## Decisions
approve, reject (final, no ladder), modify (needs modified_args, counts as approval), defer (next tier now). Only the current assignee may decide; terminal escalations refuse. Quorum: distinct responders, climbs tiers after each approval.

## Routing
candidates(tier, skill): available, open_count < max_concurrent, has skill; sorted by (open_count, id). Empty tier: Attempt with responder None, ESCALATION_REASSIGNED, next tier at no time cost. Roster: 7 people, 5 tiers.

## Aggregation and effective risk
- support = sum of supporting confidences, against = sum of contradicting ones.
- contested: supporters and detractors both non empty. confirmed: not contested and support >= 0.6. rejected: not contested, against >= 0.6, support 0.
- actionable = confirmed + contested (fed to the planner).
- _BUMP: read_only to low, low to medium, medium to high, high to critical, critical stays.

## Workers (rules)
| worker | rule |
|---|---|
| log_analyst | error_lines = int(error_rate x 1000 x 15/5); > 50 supports service_degraded (0.9); upstream top error supports upstream_fault (0.75) |
| metrics_analyst | saturated = p99 > 1000 ms, supports or contradicts service_degraded (0.95); saturated and replicas < 8 supports capacity_shortfall (0.6) |
| replication_analyst | lag > 5.0 s supports database_fault (0.95) |
| runbook_retriever | latency RB-014, errors RB-002, replication RB-031 |
| remediation_planner | scale (min(2x, 200)), restart, failover, page_vendor; ordered page_vendor 0 ... delete_volume 9 |

## Tools (15)
read_only: read_logs, read_metrics, read_replication, search_runbooks. low: restart_service, purge_cache, page_vendor, snapshot_volume. medium: scale_deployment, rollback_release, drain_node, enable_read_only. high: failover_database (irreversible, fallback enable_read_only), force_terminate (irreversible, fallback restart_service). critical: delete_volume (irreversible, fallback snapshot_volume). check_fallbacks: exists, not self, strictly lower risk; build_registry raises at import.

## Load time refusals
on_expiry missing on an approval rule; unknown on_expiry (including allow); quorum > ladder; empty ladder with approval; non positive deadline; missing risk level; roster tier with no responder; broken fallback. Policy ladder to roster cross check is a unit test over shipped configs.

## ADRs
1. Explicit state machines over a framework (own the clock, readable resume). 2. No third party deps (miniyaml). 3. Escalation is a policy, not a callback. 4. No ALLOW on expiry.

## Tests (212) and scenarios (11)
engine 43, miniyaml 24, supervisor 19, builtin tools 15, roster 14, policy 13, contested 13, cli 12, aggregator 11, journal 10, tool registry 9, scenarios 8, schema 8, clock 7, types 6. Boundary: 299 s nothing, 300 s fires. Scenarios 01 to 11: guarded cheap, medium waits, approval resumes, rejection, modify, silence exhausts, high falls back, contested raises, observe, autonomous, healthy null case.

## Bugs found
1. Contested risk bump unreachable (planner only saw confirmed). 2. Bumped risk discarded at rule lookup (empty ladder, instant exhaustion). 3. miniyaml flattened nested maps in list items (modified_args empty).

## Gaps found reading the code
Late approval accepted between deadline and tick; no resume from FROZEN; INCIDENT_RESUMED, PLAN_REVISED, AUTONOMY_CHANGED never emitted; README says 200 tests; autonomous bypasses the table for critical tools; fallback runs a medium tool without approval; no replay function.

narration.script: The problem is the approval prompt that never gets answered. An agent reaches something risky, asks, and waits. At 3am nobody replies, and now the incident has nobody watching it. So I built the escalation as its own layer. A supervisor takes an incident, sends five workers to look at logs, metrics, replication, and runbooks, and a planner proposes fixes, cheapest first. The suite caught a safety branch that could never run, because contested hypotheses never reached the planner. The limits are real. The cluster is a dataclass, the workers are rules, and nothing calls tick on a timer yet. Next is a scheduler and one LLM worker to see if the layer holds.

narration.prompt: Give me the full technical story, as you would to a staff engineer.
narration.script: The core claim is that escalation is a routing problem with deadlines, so it gets its own layer with its own state machine. Start with the tools. Each tool declares its risk, whether it's reversible, a plain words blast radius, and optionally a strictly lower risk substitute. The registry checks every substitute at import: it must exist, it can't be itself, and it must be lower risk. Failover declares read only mode. Force terminate declares a restart. The supervisor runs a static plan: four diagnostic subtasks in one batch, then remediation that depends on all four. Workers get a registry filtered to read only tools, so they can't reach a mutating tool by name. The aggregator sums confidence per hypothesis on each side and tracks who said what. Contested means both sides have a voice, not that the net is small, because two confident opposites and two weak signals both net to zero. Confirmed and contested hypotheses both go to the planner, and any action addressing a contested one gets its risk bumped a level. Then the escalation. The policy is a YAML table by risk. Medium asks primary then secondary with 300 seconds and escalates on silence. High asks three tiers with 180 seconds and falls back on silence. Critical needs two signatures with 600 seconds and holds. raise_for picks the rule by the effective risk. That lookup used to use the declared risk, which gave a contested restart an empty ladder and an instant exhaustion. Routing filters the tier by skill and capacity and sorts by load. Later tiers get half the window with a 30 second floor. Decisions are approve, reject, modify, and defer. Reject is final. Modify needs arguments. Quorum climbs tiers and requires different people. tick is caller driven against an injected clock, which is the reason I wrote the state machines by hand. A framework's interrupt waits indefinitely and owns its scheduler. On expiry, deny drops the action. Safe fallback runs the substitute with narrowed arguments and records approved by timeout fallback. Escalate moves a tier or exhausts. Hold freezes. There's no allow, and a test asserts it. The supervisor never blocks. It returns awaiting human, and the next advance resumes on the same step, which one scenario pins so diagnosis never reruns. Everything goes to an append only journal with a closed event vocabulary. Testing is 212 unittest cases and 11 YAML scenarios that each state why they exist, run on a bare interpreter across three Python versions. The suite caught two design flaws during the build. The risk bump for contested diagnoses was unreachable, because the planner was only fed confirmed hypotheses, so no proposal ever addressed a contested one. It read like a guarantee and did nothing. My hand written YAML reader also flattened nested maps inside list items, which silently emptied the edited arguments in a scenario. Reading it back, I'd fix four things. An approval can land after its deadline if tick hasn't run. Frozen runs can't resume. The fallback runs a medium tool without approval. And autonomous mode bypasses the table for critical tools. Production needs a scheduler, persistence, a pager on the subscribe hook, and an LLM worker to test the open question.

narration.prompt: Explain it to someone who is not an engineer.
narration.script: When software runs into something risky, like switching a company's main database, it's supposed to stop and ask a person. Most systems then just wait. If it's the middle of the night and nobody answers, the problem keeps getting worse while the software sits there. I built a system where every one of those requests goes to a specific person with a deadline, and the rules for what happens if they stay silent are written down ahead of time. It might ask the next person up, or do a safer version of the action, or freeze everything until someone looks. It never treats silence as a yes. I tested it with 212 automated checks on a pretend computer system, so the next step is trying it with real AI agents.

narration.prompt: What happens if the approval arrives one second after the deadline?
narration.script: It depends on whether tick has run. tick is caller driven. If the deadline passed but nobody has called tick yet, the escalation is still assigned, and decide accepts the approval. If tick already ran, the escalation has moved on. On escalate, the old responder is no longer the assignee, so their decision is refused. On fallback or deny, it's terminal and decide raises. That first window is a real gap, and it's on my list of missing scenarios. The fix is one line in decide: compare the clock to the attempt's deadline and refuse, or expire first. I'd want the scheduler's tick interval in the record too, since it widens every deadline in practice.

narration.prompt: How would you make this survive a process restart?
narration.script: Today it can't. Incident runs and escalations live in memory, and the journal's JSON lines sink is the only thing on disk. I'd make the events the source of truth. Every state change is already a closed set of events, so I'd write them to a durable store and rebuild escalations and runs by replaying them on startup. The journal docstring claims that's possible, but there's no replay function yet, so I'd write that first and test it by replaying every scenario's events and comparing state. Then decide needs compare and set on the escalation's state, so two approvers or two schedulers can't both win.

narration.prompt: How would you plug in an LLM worker, and what would you measure?
narration.script: I'd implement the Worker protocol, which is a name, a capability set, and a handle method, over one analyst, say metrics. It gets the same read only registry, so it can't reach a mutating tool even if it names one. Its findings need a confidence and the hypotheses they support or contradict, so I'd constrain the output to that schema and reject anything else. Then I'd run each scenario many times and measure how often contested fires, whether the expected actions still run, and whether anything runs that shouldn't. The escalation layer shouldn't change at all. If contested fires constantly, I'd add a minimum confidence before a finding counts as a voice.

narration.prompt: Why does high risk get a shorter deadline than medium?
narration.script: Because high has a cheap, safe answer to silence and medium doesn't. Every high risk tool in the registry declares a strictly safer substitute, so if nobody answers in 180 seconds, the system does the conservative thing and keeps going. Medium escalates on silence, so a longer first window means fewer needless second pages. Critical gets the longest, 600 seconds, plus two signatures, because its answer to silence is to freeze. So the deadline is set by what silence costs at that level, not by how dangerous the action sounds. Later tiers get half the window, because by then the incident has already used up the earlier ones.

narration.prompt: Your fallback runs a medium risk action nobody approved. That's allow with extra steps.
narration.script: It's a fair hit, and it's true that read only mode is medium and runs without anyone approving it on timeout. What's different is what runs and what the record says. The substitute was declared by the tool's author, checked at import to be strictly lower risk, and chosen by whoever wrote the high risk row of the policy. And the journal records approved by timeout fallback, so nobody can mistake it for a decision. If I tightened it, I'd require every fallback to sit below the escalation bar, and enforce that when the registry loads.

narration.script: Both true, and I put both in the limitations. The cluster is a dataclass and no model is called. What I'd push back on is that the hard part is the cluster. The part people get wrong is what happens when the human doesn't answer, and that's real code with 212 tests, tested to the exact second. The world is a seam: each tool's run function takes the world and validated arguments, so swapping in real APIs doesn't touch the escalation layer. The workers are a seam too. cards.q: What problem does handoff solve, in one sentence and then technically?
cards.easy: When an automated system asks a human to approve something risky and nobody answers, most systems just wait forever; handoff decides in advance who gets asked, how long they have, and exactly what happens if they stay silent.
cards.deep: The common human in the loop shape is a blocking confirm() call: it does not say who is asked, it has no deadline, and the case where it never returns is undefined. During an incident at 3am that undefined case is the normal case, and an agent parked on an unanswered prompt is worse than one that never asked, because nothing is watching the incident. handoff treats escalation as a routing problem: a policy table keyed by risk names the tiers that may approve, the first tier's deadline, the quorum, the required skill, and a mandatory on_expiry behaviour (deny, safe_fallback, escalate, hold). A roster supplies people with tiers, skills, and load limits. A caller driven tick() fires deadlines. The domain is incident response on a simulated cluster with five rule based workers, and the README says plainly that the domain is not the point; the escalation layer is.
cards.say: Most human in the loop is a modal dialog that waits forever. I built the case nobody designs for: the page goes out at 3am and nobody answers. Every escalation in handoff has an owner, a deadline, and a written rule for silence.
evidence: portfolio: Most human in the loop is a modal dialog that blocks forever.

cards.q: How does handoff relate to comms-agent?
cards.easy: comms-agent added a review gate where a person checks low confidence items before a report goes out. That covers the case where the reviewer shows up. handoff covers the case where they do not.
cards.deep: In comms-agent the human in the loop gate is a pause inside an agent graph: flag the uncertain items, let a reviewer correct them, then continue. Its implicit assumption is that the reviewer eventually acts. handoff makes the opposite assumption the design center: the reviewer may never act, so every question carries a deadline and a declared consequence for silence, and the escalation logic gets its own layer (roster, policy, engine, journal) instead of being a node in the graph. The write up calls the no show case the one that breaks these systems in production.
cards.say: comms-agent answered what happens when the reviewer shows up. handoff answers what happens when they don't, which is the case that actually breaks in production. So the escalation became its own layer with deadlines, instead of a pause inside a graph.
evidence: portfolio: handoff covers what happens when they do not, which is the case that breaks these systems in production.

cards.q: Describe the supervisor orchestration loop.
cards.easy: The supervisor moves each incident through fixed stages: plan, send work out, merge results, decide, act, check whether it worked. If it needs a person, it stops and returns, and the caller resumes it later from the same spot.
cards.deep: Supervisor.advance(run) loops while run.state is not terminal, with a guard that abandons the run after 100 iterations. States: TRIAGE to PLANNING; PLANNING builds a static plan (four diagnostic subtasks plus one remediation subtask that depends on them); DISPATCHING runs ready subtasks in dependency batches; AGGREGATING merges findings and journals CONFLICT_DETECTED for each contested hypothesis; DECIDING drops proposals whose addressed hypothesis is neither confirmed nor contested and closes the run if nothing is left; ACTING takes the head of the queue, computes effective risk, and either blocks it (POLICY_BLOCKED), escalates it (AWAITING_HUMAN), or executes it; VERIFYING reads metrics and resolves if p99 is no longer saturated, otherwise tries the next queued action or abandons. Terminal states are RESOLVED, FROZEN, ABANDONED. advance() never blocks: in AWAITING_HUMAN it checks the escalation and returns if it is still open, so calling it again while blocked changes nothing.
cards.say: advance() drives the incident as far as it can without a human, then returns. If it's waiting on a person, it returns AWAITING_HUMAN and the caller drives the clock. Calling it again while blocked is a no op, which a test checks.

cards.q: Define the supervisor pattern, a worker, and capability routing as used here.
cards.easy: A supervisor is one coordinator that hands subtasks to specialist workers and decides what to do with their answers. A worker answers one kind of question. Routing by capability means a subtask asks for a skill, like metrics, and gets whichever worker offers it.
cards.deep: The Worker protocol is three members: name, a capabilities frozenset, and handle(subtask, ctx) returning a WorkerResult of findings (claims with confidence and the hypotheses they support or contradict) and proposals (actions with the hypothesis they address). WorkerRegistry.for_capability returns the alphabetically first worker claiming the capability, so swapping a worker is a registration change, not a planner edit. Workers never execute; the supervisor is the only caller of mutating tools, which is what makes the escalation ladder load bearing rather than advisory. A worker exception is caught, journaled as SUBTASK_FAILED, and marks the aggregate degraded, so a crashed worker degrades the run instead of ending it. Replacing a rule based analyst with an LLM backed one means implementing the same protocol.

cards.q: What do the five workers actually do?
cards.easy: Three analysts read logs, metrics, and database replication and report what they see. A runbook retriever looks up a matching procedure. A planner turns the confirmed or disputed explanations into proposed fixes, cheapest first.
cards.deep: LogAnalyst: read_logs over 15 minutes; error_lines = int(error_rate x 1000 x window/5); more than 50 lines supports service_degraded at confidence 0.9, otherwise contradicts it; an unhealthy service's top error ('upstream timeout calling payments') supports upstream_fault at 0.75. MetricsAnalyst: saturated means p99 above 1000 ms; supports or contradicts service_degraded at 0.95, and saturated with under 8 replicas supports capacity_shortfall at 0.6. ReplicationAnalyst: lag above LAG_THRESHOLD_S = 5.0 supports database_fault at 0.95, else contradicts. RunbookRetriever: keyword match on the symptom (latency to RB-014, errors to RB-002, replication to RB-031). RemediationPlanner: capacity_shortfall to scale_deployment (replicas min(2x current, 200)), service_degraded to restart_service, database_fault to failover_database on the first replica, upstream_fault to page_vendor; sorted by a fixed order with page_vendor 0, purge_cache 1, restart 2, scale 3, rollback 4, enable_read_only 5, drain 6, failover 7, force_terminate 8, delete_volume 9, so the reversible, narrow action is tried first. All thresholds are hand written; no model is called.

cards.q: Why hand workers a read only tool registry instead of trusting them not to call mutating tools?
cards.easy: Because a rule a worker is trusted to follow is a rule that one bug or one bad model output can break. If the dangerous tools are not in the worker's registry at all, the worker cannot call them even by name.
cards.deep: Supervisor._readonly_tools builds a fresh ToolRegistry containing only tools whose risk is READ_ONLY, and WorkerContext.call resolves names only against that registry, so a worker asking for failover_database gets UnknownToolError. This is capability based security: authority is what you hold a reference to. It is the property that keeps the escalation ladder meaningful once a worker is an LLM, since a model can be prompted into naming any tool. test_workers_cannot_see_mutating_tools pins it. The tradeoff is that a worker cannot do a safe write like attaching a note, which would need its own risk class.
cards.say: Workers get a registry with only read only tools in it. They can't call a mutating tool even by name. With rule based workers that's tidy, but it's the property that matters once a worker is a model, because a model can be talked into naming anything.

cards.q: How is the plan built and dispatched?
cards.easy: The plan is fixed: check logs, metrics, replication, and runbooks in parallel, then ask the planner for fixes once all four are done. The planner is told which explanations survived so far.
cards.deep: planner.plan() emits subtasks for DIAGNOSTIC_CAPABILITIES (logs, metrics, replication, runbook) with service and symptom args, then a remediation subtask whose depends_on is all four ids. planner.ready() returns subtasks whose dependencies are all done, so dispatch runs batch one (four diagnostics) then batch two (remediation). Before the remediation worker runs, the supervisor aggregates the results so far and injects interim.actionable(0.6), confirmed plus contested hypotheses, into its args. The static plan is a deliberate choice: the same incident always fans out the same way, so a change in outcome is a change in the world or the policy, never in the plan. ADR 0001 names a dynamic per incident plan as the change that would justify moving to a graph framework.

cards.q: How does the aggregator decide a hypothesis is confirmed, contested, or rejected?
cards.easy: Each worker's finding says which explanations it supports and which it contradicts, with a confidence. The aggregator adds those up per explanation and tracks who said what. If both sides have at least one voice, the explanation is contested.
cards.deep: For each hypothesis: support is the sum of confidences of findings that support it, against the sum of those that contradict it, with supporters and detractors as the sets of worker names. contested is true when both sets are non empty. confirmed means not contested and support at least the threshold (0.6). rejected means not contested, against at least 0.6, and zero support. actionable is confirmed plus contested, so a disputed explanation still gets a concrete proposal for a human to judge. Findings validate their own inputs: confidence must be in 0 to 1 and a finding cannot support and contradict the same hypothesis. Failed workers are excluded from the sums and flag the aggregate as degraded. Note support is a sum, so two agreeing workers can exceed 1.0; it is an evidence weight, not a probability.

cards.q: Why define contested by voices on both sides instead of a small net score?
cards.easy: Two confident workers reaching opposite conclusions and two unsure workers giving weak signals both net out near zero, but only the first is a real disagreement that should stop the system.
cards.deep: A net score rule (support minus against near zero) cannot tell 0.9 versus 0.8 from 0.05 versus 0.04. The aggregator docstring gives exactly that example and test_contest_is_about_voices_not_net_score pins it. The common alternatives, averaging, taking the max confidence, or letting a model reconcile the findings in a summary, all hide the disagreement, and a hidden disagreement is the state in which an automated system should not act alone. The cost of the voices rule is sensitivity: any single detractor contests a hypothesis, so a noisy worker could force escalations; a production version might require each side to clear a minimum confidence before it counts as a voice.
cards.say: I didn't want averaging. Two confident workers disagreeing and two weak signals both net to zero, but only one of them should stop the machine. So contested means both sides have a voice. The flip side is one noisy worker can force escalations, which I'd gate with a minimum confidence.

cards.q: How does disagreement change what happens to an action?
cards.easy: Any action aimed at a disputed explanation is treated as one risk level more dangerous. That can push a cheap action, like a service restart, over the line where a person must approve it.
cards.deep: Supervisor.effective_risk returns the tool's declared risk, bumped through _BUMP (read_only to low, low to medium, medium to high, high to critical, critical stays critical) when the proposal's addresses field names a contested hypothesis. The bumped level is passed into engine.raise_for(risk=...), and the escalation's reason gets '(risk raised to medium: the diagnosis is contested)' so the human sees why. The journal's ACTION_PROPOSED carries both declared_risk and effective_risk. The design claim is that uncertainty about the diagnosis and danger in the fix are different problems with the same remedy, so one mechanism covers both.
cards.say: If the workers disagree about the diagnosis, any fix for it gets bumped one risk level. So a restart that would normally just run now asks a human. Same remedy for two kinds of uncertainty, one mechanism.

cards.q: How does routing pick a person to page?
cards.easy: It looks at the current tier on the ladder, keeps the people who have the needed skill and spare capacity, and pages the least busy one. If nobody on that tier can take it, it moves to the next tier immediately.
cards.deep: Responder has id, name, tier, skills, available, max_concurrent (default 2), open_count. Roster.candidates(tier, skill) filters to has_capacity (available and open_count < max_concurrent) and can_approve(skill), then sorts by (open_count, id), so the spread is even and deterministic. _assign takes the first candidate not already in esc.approvals (so quorum needs distinct people), acquires it (open_count += 1), appends an Attempt with the deadline, and journals ESCALATION_ASSIGNED. With an empty pool it appends an Attempt with responder_id None, journals ESCALATION_REASSIGNED 'no responder with capacity on this tier', increments tier_index, and loops, so an empty tier costs no time; past the last tier it exhausts. Capacity is released on resolution, expiry, defer, and per approval when climbing for quorum. The shipped roster is seven people across five tiers; for a high risk page, ana and bo (both primary, both with infrastructure) are tied at zero load and ana wins on id.

cards.q: How long does each tier get?
cards.easy: The first person gets the full time from the policy. Each later tier gets half as long as the one before, but never less than 30 seconds, because by then the incident has already burned through the earlier windows.
cards.deep: $w_k = \max\left(30, \lfloor d \cdot b^{k} \rfloor\right)$ seconds, where $d$ is the rule's deadline_seconds, $k$ is tier_index, and $b$ is the engine's backoff, 0.5 by default (the engine tests build it with 1.0 to keep windows equal). Applied to the shipped policy (Tanay's arithmetic from the code): medium 300 s then 150 s; high 180, 90, 45 s; critical 600, 300, 150 s. Because tier_index also advances past empty tiers, a skipped tier still shrinks the next window. The reasoning in Escalation.next_deadline's docstring: later tiers get shorter windows because the remaining urgency is higher. The shorter later windows only matter when an escalation actually climbs: on silence for medium, or after a defer, a skipped tier, or a first approval toward quorum. High falls back after its first 180 s of silence rather than climbing, so its 90 and 45 second windows apply only to defers and skipped tiers. A defensible alternative is a fixed total budget split across tiers, which bounds the worst case time to a decision.

cards.q: What can a human say to an escalation, and how is each handled?
cards.easy: Approve, reject, modify, or defer. Reject is final. Modify approves with edited arguments. Defer hands it to the next tier right away.
cards.deep: EscalationEngine.decide(id, responder_id, decision, note, modified_args): refuses a terminal escalation (ValueError), refuses a responder who is not the current assignee, records the decision on the latest Attempt, journals ESCALATION_DECIDED with the responder as actor. REJECT: REJECTED, release everyone, final; the asymmetry is deliberate, since one person saying no is enough to stop an irreversible action while one yes may not be enough to start it. DEFER: next tier immediately, releasing the deferrer. MODIFY: requires modified_args (ValueError otherwise), stores them, and counts as an approval; effective_args then returns the edited args. APPROVE or MODIFY appends the responder to approvals and resolves when the quorum is met. Scenario 05 shows why modify exists: an on call engineer agreeing with the diagnosis but not the number (9 replicas instead of 12) would otherwise reject and do it by hand, and the system would learn nothing.

cards.q: How does quorum work for critical actions?
cards.easy: Critical actions need two different people to approve. After the first yes, the request climbs to the next tier for a second signature, and a single no at any point stops it.
cards.deep: critical: quorum 2, ladder incident_commander, engineering_manager, director. On APPROVE with approvals below quorum, the engine increments tier_index, releases the approver, and _assign pages the next tier, excluding anyone already in approvals, so the same person cannot supply both signatures. One rejection after one approval still stops it. If the ladder runs out before the quorum is met, the escalation exhausts. Load time validation rejects a quorum larger than the ladder because it could never be satisfied. On silence, critical holds. cards.q: Describe the escalation state machine.
cards.easy: An escalation starts pending, becomes assigned when someone is paged, and ends approved, rejected, fell back, denied on timeout, exhausted, or held. Held is the odd one: it is not finished, but its clock has stopped.
cards.deep: States: PENDING, ASSIGNED, APPROVED, REJECTED, FELL_BACK, DENIED_ON_TIMEOUT, HELD, EXHAUSTED. Transitions: raise_for creates PENDING and _assign moves it to ASSIGNED (or straight to EXHAUSTED when no tier has anyone). From ASSIGNED: approve or modify with quorum met to APPROVED; approve below quorum or defer to ASSIGNED on the next tier (or EXHAUSTED); reject to REJECTED; tick on an overdue attempt applies on_expiry to ASSIGNED on the next tier, EXHAUSTED, FELL_BACK, DENIED_ON_TIMEOUT, or HELD. is_open covers PENDING, ASSIGNED, HELD; everything else is terminal and decide() refuses it. resolution() maps APPROVED to run the original with effective args, FELL_BACK to run the fallback, everything else to not run. One inconsistency to know: ADR 0001 describes six terminal states, while the code and the engine docstring treat HELD as open.

cards.q: How does the journal work, and is it really write before act?
cards.easy: Every state change becomes an event from a fixed list, appended to an in memory log and optionally to a JSON lines file, and passed to any subscribers. Intent is recorded before execution, though the executed event itself is written after the tool runs.
cards.deep: EventKind is a closed StrEnum (incident, plan, subtask, findings, conflict, action, escalation, policy, autonomy kinds), so a new kind of event is a deliberate code change. Event has kind, incident_id, at, detail, id, actor. Journal.append stores it, writes one sorted key JSON object per line when a sink is set, then calls subscribers; a raising subscriber propagates after the event is recorded, because a pager that silently fails is the same as no pager. Write before act, precisely: ACTION_PROPOSED is journaled before any escalation or execution, ESCALATION_* events precede the effects they describe, and the fallback's ACTION_ALLOWED precedes its execution; but in _execute the tool runs and then ACTION_EXECUTED is appended, so a crash mid tool leaves 'proposed' without 'executed', which is the recoverable 'about to' state the docstring describes. The journal docstring also claims replayability; no replay function exists yet. Three declared kinds (INCIDENT_RESUMED, PLAN_REVISED, AUTONOMY_CHANGED) are never emitted.

cards.q: Why hand write the state machines instead of using LangGraph or another agent framework?
cards.easy: Because the transition table is the interesting part of the project, and a framework puts a layer between the reader and it. It also keeps control of the clock, so deadlines can be tested to the second.
cards.deep: ADR 0001 concedes the case for a framework (less code, known vocabulary, a visualizer) and argues against it on two specifics: pause and resume on the same step is the behaviour most likely to be subtly wrong, and writing it out means a reviewer checks one file instead of trusting a checkpointer they cannot see; and frameworks tend to own the scheduler, which makes deadlines untestable at 299 versus 300 seconds. LangGraph's interrupt pauses until resumed with no built in timeout, needs a checkpointer and thread id, and reruns the interrupted node from its start on resume. The ADR calls the decision reversible because node names and persisted state map onto LangGraph directly, and says to revisit it if the plan becomes dynamic per incident. Costs it names: no visualizer, no community, and a long advance() method with a loop guard.

cards.q: Why is escalation a policy rather than a callback?
cards.easy: A callback blocks a thread, does not say who is asked, and has no deadline. A policy table says who, how long, and what happens on silence, and anyone can read and review it.
cards.deep: ADR 0003 lists three failures of confirm(action): it blocks (a thread parked six hours is a resource leak with a human attached), it does not route (whoever is at the terminal answers, with no notion of tier, skill, or load), and it has no deadline (the never returns case is undefined). The decision: a declarative table keyed by risk; raise_for records the question and returns immediately; tick fires deadlines; the supervisor returns AWAITING_HUMAN and the caller drives the clock. Consequences: the policy is diffable after an incident review, load time validation catches incident time failures, and the whole system is testable with ManualClock and no sleeps. Cost, stated in the ADR and README: a deployment needs a real scheduler calling tick, and none is written.

cards.q: Why not just use LangGraph's interrupt for human in the loop?
cards.easy: LangGraph's interrupt pauses a graph and waits until someone resumes it. It has no deadline, no routing, and no rule for silence, which are the three things this project is about. Those would have to be built either way.
cards.deep: Concede: LangGraph would give persistence through a checkpointer, a known vocabulary, and a visualizer, and ADR 0001 says node names and persisted state map onto it directly. Defend: per its docs, interrupt() waits indefinitely until resumed, needs a checkpointer and thread id, and reruns the interrupted node from its start on resume, so pre interrupt side effects must be idempotent. None of that answers who is paged, by when, or what happens on silence. handoff's engine is that missing layer, and owning the clock is what lets the tests hit 299 and 300 seconds exactly. If the plan became dynamic per incident, Tanay would move the supervisor onto a graph framework and keep the escalation engine as is.

cards.q: What would production need, and what breaks at 10x and 100x?

cards.q: What would you build next?
cards.easy: A scheduler for tick, one LLM backed worker to test the open question, a pager on the journal hook, roster rotations, and scenarios for competing incidents and late approvals.
cards.deep: The order in CLAUDE.md, by how much each improves the project: (1) a scheduler for tick, the most honest gap; (2) one LLM backed worker implementing Worker over an existing analyst, run repeatedly to see whether contested detection and the scenario expectations hold under nondeterminism; (3) a notification channel on Journal.subscribe; (4) roster rotation with schedules, time zones, and handover; (5) scenarios for concurrent incidents competing for one responder and for an approval that arrives after the deadline fired. Tanay would add two from reading the code: a resume path from FROZEN, and an autonomy ceiling for irreversible tools. Deferred on purpose: a real cluster integration (World is the seam and a run signature away) and an approvals web UI (the Decision API is what a UI would call).

cards.q: Compare three human in the loop designs: a blocking confirm, a graph interrupt, and handoff's escalation engine.
cards.easy: A blocking confirm waits forever for whoever is at the screen. A graph interrupt saves state and waits forever for someone to resume it. handoff pages a specific person with a deadline and a written rule for silence.
cards.deep: Blocking confirm(): holds a thread, no routing, no deadline, silent case undefined, testable only with mocks or real waiting. Graph interrupt (for example LangGraph): state checkpointed so nothing blocks, resume via a command, but no built in deadline or routing, and the interrupted node reruns from its start on resume. handoff: raise_for returns immediately; routing by tier, skill, and load; a deadline per attempt with shrinking windows; quorum; one of four declared silence behaviours; a caller driven tick testable to the second; an audit record of every attempt. What handoff lacks that a framework has: durable checkpointing, a scheduler, a visualizer, and community support.

cards.q: Define blast radius, reversibility, quorum, autonomy level, and audit trail as this project uses them.
cards.easy: Blast radius is a plain words description of what can break. Reversibility says whether the action can be undone. Quorum is how many different people must approve. Autonomy level is how much the operator lets the system do alone. The audit trail is the permanent record of every question, answer, and silence.
cards.deep: blast_radius is a string on each Tool, copied into every Escalation and shown to the human, written without jargon, for example 'every writer reconnects, in flight transactions are lost'; a test asserts every tool declares one. reversible is a bool on Tool; irreversible tools must be high or critical and declare a fallback (both pinned by tests), and the planner orders reversible actions first. quorum is per policy rule (2 for critical) and needs distinct responders. Autonomy is observe, suggest, guarded, or autonomous, applied on top of the table. The audit trail is the append only Journal plus each Escalation's attempts and audit() rendering; the reason there is no allow on expiry is to keep that trail honest about who decided.

cards.q: Explain handoff to a hiring manager for an AI engineering role.
cards.easy: Agents that ask people for approval usually wait forever. Tanay built the layer that decides who to ask, how long they get, and what happens if they never answer, and tested it to the second.
cards.deep: Lead with the 3am failover story, then the four expiry behaviours and the missing allow, then the numbers with the simulation caveat, then the open question about LLM workers.
cards.say: I built the escalation layer for agents that need human approval. Every request has an owner, a deadline, and a rule for silence. If nobody answers a database failover in 180 seconds, it puts the database in read only mode instead, and the log says nobody answered. There are 212 tests and no dependencies. It runs on a simulated cluster with rule based workers, and whether it holds up with LLM workers is the next thing I'd test.

cards.q: Explain the deadline design to a staff engineer.
cards.easy: Time is injected, tick is caller driven, nothing blocks or sleeps, and every expiry behaviour is pinned at its boundary second.
cards.deep: Clock protocol with SystemClock and ManualClock; tick fires overdue ASSIGNED escalations and applies on_expiry; windows shrink by a 0.5 backoff with a 30 second floor; supervisor returns AWAITING_HUMAN; the missing piece is a scheduler and persistence.
cards.say: Every deadline is measured against an injected clock, and tick is driven by the caller, so nothing sleeps. Tests advance a manual clock 299 seconds and assert nothing fired, then one more and assert it did. Later tiers get half the window, floored at 30 seconds. What's missing is the scheduler that calls tick in production, and persistence so open escalations survive a restart.

cards.q: Explain it to a product manager.
cards.easy: When automation needs permission and the person is asleep, something still has to happen. handoff makes that something a decision written down in advance, and it never pretends silence was a yes.
cards.deep: Frame it as reliability of approvals: who is asked, how long they have, a safer fallback, and an honest record. Mention that the rules live in a readable file a non engineer can review.
cards.say: Picture an automated system that needs a person's OK at 3am and nobody picks up. Most products just wait. Mine decides ahead of time: ask the right person, give them a deadline, and if they're silent, do the safer thing or freeze, never the risky thing. The rules live in a readable file, so an ops lead can review them without reading code.

cards.q: Define failover, read only mode, mutating tool, tier, ladder, and on call roster.
cards.easy: A failover switches the main database to a backup copy. Read only mode keeps the database answering reads but refuses writes. A mutating tool is any action that changes the system. A tier is a level of responders, a ladder is the order tiers are asked in, and the roster lists who is on call at each tier.
cards.deep: failover_database promotes a replica to primary and demotes the old primary; in the World model it bumps failovers and resets lag, and the blast radius is that every writer reconnects and in flight transactions are lost, which is why it is irreversible and high. enable_read_only sets database.read_only, so writes are rejected and checkout degrades, but data is safe and a human can undo it, which makes it the declared fallback. Mutating means any tool above READ_ONLY; only the supervisor may call one. Tiers in the shipped roster: primary, secondary, incident_commander, engineering_manager, director. A policy ladder lists tiers in paging order per risk level. The roster is static: seven people with skills and max_concurrent load limits, no rotation schedule, time zones, or handover.

cards.q: Define a state machine, an injectable clock, an append only log, a closed event vocabulary, and a seam, as used here.
cards.easy: A state machine lists the states something can be in and the allowed moves between them. An injectable clock is time passed in as an object, so tests can control it. An append only log never edits or deletes entries. A closed vocabulary means every event type is listed in one place. A seam is a spot where a real component can replace a simulated one without touching the rest.
cards.deep: State machines: RunState for incidents (eleven states, three terminal) and EscalationState for escalations (eight states); both are hand written per ADR 0001 and refuse undefined transitions (decide on a terminal escalation raises). Injectable clock: the Clock protocol with SystemClock and ManualClock; nothing else calls datetime.now and nothing sleeps. Append only log: Journal.append is the only write, with an optional JSON lines sink. Closed vocabulary: EventKind is a StrEnum, so a new kind of event is a deliberate code change rather than a free string at a call site. Seams named in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md: the World object (swap each tool's run for a real API call), the Worker protocol (swap a rule based analyst for an LLM one), and the static planner (swap for a generated plan, which ADR 0001 says would justify a framework).
